Vs.

full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-opposite parties' case, in short, is that the suit properties originally belonged to one Kashem Ali and after his death his sons namely, Wahed Ali, Alimuddin, Hasen Ali, Abdul Jabbar and Sabor Ali inherited the suit land which has been described in Schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' of the plaint. Wahed Ali died leaving one son Md Idris (plaintiff-opposite party No. 1) and one daughter namely, Sharbatunnessa (defendant No. 1 opposite party No. 7) Alimuddin died leaving only one daughter namely, Latifa Khatoon (defendant No. 2, present petitioner No. 1). Hasan Ali died leaving 2 sons namely, Mohammad Ali and Ahmed Ali and 4 daughters namely, Safura Khatoon, Ohida Khatoon, Noor Jahan, Shahida. Khatoon (defendants-petitioner Nos. 4 to 7). Abdul Jabbar died leaving 3 sons namely, Md Khalilur Rahman, Md Ashek Ali and Md Sirajul Islam and 2 daughters namely, Fatema Begum and Saleha Begum (defendant petitioner Nos. 8 to 12) and that they inherited schedule 'Ka', 'Kha' and 'Ga' land. Then Sabar Ali Master died issue less leaving behind 4 brothers who were jointly owning and possessing in the suit land in ejmali after the death of their father Kashem Ali. Thereafter, all the petitioners and opposite parties inherited the suit land according to Muslim Law. Both the plaintiffs and defendants have been in their actual physical possession and ownership of their said ancestral lands in Ejmali and accordingly by way of exercising all rights, title, interest and possession. Before the partition of the said entire suit land by metes and bounds, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in connivance with his other sons i.e. opposite party Nos. 2 to 6, fraudulently created a so-called Wasiatnama in their home on 4-1-1987, although Sabar Ali died on 1-12-1986 as per Annexures A and B in respect of the entire land of said Sabar Ali measuring 1.75 acres i.e. probable share of Sabar Ali, with an ulterior motive to grab the same by way of forged and false personification. The learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur decreed in part the Title Suit No. 41 of 1988 by judgment and decree dated 30-9-1999 which was affirmed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur by judgment and decree dated 22-7-1997 passed in Title Appeal No. 169 of 1990. 

 The impugned judgment in Title Appeal No. 169 of 1990 was delivered on 22-7-1997 and the decree was drawn on 29-7-1997 and application for obtaining certified copies of those judgment and decree was filed on 26-8-1997 but the said certified copies of the judgments and decrees were supplied on 15-10-1997 and accordingly, the petitioners were contemplating to come before this Court in revisional jurisdiction but the relations, local elites and well-wishers of both petitioners and the opposite parties came forward to arrive at an amicable settlement in between both the parties as there was a severe apprehension of grave consequence which would have to be faced by either party who are relations to each other. Out of the two controversial death certificates, one is dated 1-12-1986 obtained by the petitioners, which indicates that the controversial will (Wasiatnama) was created by the plaintiff-opposite party on 4-14987 by way of false personification after the death of the testator Shabor Ali Master. Subsequently, the plaintiffs-opposite parties tried to prove otherwise by oral evidence. Accordingly, there were several salishes of local people before and after the disposal of the above cases as per impugned judgments. In pursuance with the said last date of talk of compromise there was a salish on 5-11-1999 and on 23-11-1999 on the basis of two sittings but without any final settlement. The local friends, relations and well-wishers gave their final report on 12-11-1999 stating, inter alia, that they ultimately failed to settle the matter and there is a delay of 830 days in filing the instant revisional application by swearing affidavit being Entry No. 46063 dated 23-11-1999 only after 11 days of said last date of fruitless compromise and after 831 days delay of last date of Judgment of Title Appeal No. 169 of 1990 in which the judgment and decree was delivered on 22-7-1997. This delay was due to all the said 25 signatories of the local elites in the said application, of compromise from both sides dated 5-11-1997. It is further stated that the defendants-petitioners could not come before this Court against the judgment and decree dated 22-7-1997 as there was a false and malafide hope of so-called compromise and, as such, there was a delay of 831 days in filing the revisional application which are required to be condoned. 

 4. The plaintiff-opposite parties filed a counter-affidavit denying the statement made in the application for condonation of delay stating, inter alia, that the statements made in paragraph 5 are incorrect, vague, unspecified and no date, time and place have been given as to the so-called statement for compromise of dispute. In fact, there was no proposal of settlement of dispute and none of the locality gathered together to settle the matter out of Court at any point of time. It is further a cause of action nor sufficient cause shown or given by the petitioners in the application for condonation of delay. The petitioners are required to explain the cause of delay of each day by sufficient cause but there is no such explanation in the instant case and, as such, the delay of 729 days occurred as appeared in the prayer portion of the application of delay of 830 days as appeared in paragraph 6 of the application was not reasonably explained while filing the revisional application. The application for condonation of delay has not been prepared and filed in form and, as such, the same is liable to be rejected and, as such, the Rule should be discharged. 

 5. Mr ASM Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the heirs of the late Kashem Ali, the defendant-petitioners, being prevented from filing revisional application before this Court by the plaintiffs-opposite parties with the help of local friends, relations and well-wishers in the name of negotiation and thereby killed time and fraudulently misled the defendants-petitioners from filing the revisional application within the time without having any compromise and thus a delay of 830 days occurred in filing the revisional application against the Judgment and decree dated 22-7-1997 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 169 of 1990. He further submits that the delay is unintentional and beyond the control of the petitioners. He then submits that the petitioners will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the delay is not condoned and, as such, the Rule should he made absolute. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has cited before me the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Pabna vs Md Kobad Ali and others reported in 39 DLR 205 where it has been held that there is no period of limitation for a revisional application although the residuary article 181 has prescribed a period of three years for an application. He also cited the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) vs Md Khairullah and another reported in 49 DLR 118 and also decision reported in 16 DLR (AD) 386. 

 7. I have perused the application for condonation of delay with the supplementary affidavit, counter-affidavit filed on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 and other materials-on-record. Admittedly, the judgment and decree was passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur on 22-7-1997 and the decree was drawn on 29-7-1997 in Title Appeal No. 169 of 1990. The petitioners in the application for condonation of delay in paragraph 6 stated that there was a delay of 831 days in filing the revisional application which is required to be condoned, whereas from the prayer portion of the application it appears that he prayed for condonation of delay for 729 days and the Rule was also issued to that effect. In the supplementary affidavit the petitioners stated that there was a delay of 831 days in filing the revisional application and out of which 139 days should be deducted thereby delay stands for 692 days, which was required to be condoned. In the instant case admittedly, the judgment and decree was delivered on 22-7-1997 and decree was signed on 29-7-1997 and the petitioners preferred the revisional application and the application for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act swearing an affidavit on 23-11-1999. According to the Stamp Reporter, there was a delay of 729 days in filing the revisional application. In the instant case before us, defendant-petitioners in some part of the application for condonation of delay mentioned delay of 729 days and in some other portion mentioned delay of 831 days and from the supplementary-affidavit also it appears that the petitioners prayed for condonation of delay of 692 days or 839 days. From the aforesaid statements made by the petitioners it appears that the petitioner is not sure about the exact number of days of delay occurred in preferring the revisional application. A party seeking condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act must satisfy the Court that it had not been negligent and have been perusing the case most diligently and carefully. The petitioners are under a legal duty to give sufficient explanation of each and every day of delay. While considering the prayer for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, the question of reasonable excuse of sufficient cause within the meaning of section 5 of the Limitation Act should be shown which means the default on the part of the petitioners is not deliberate and it was beyond the control of the petitioners and that he has pursued the matter with good faith and due diligence. The party seeking condonation under section 5 of the Limitation Act must satisfy the Court that it has not been negligent and rather he has been pursuing the case with due diligence. The court of law can exercise jurisdiction under section 5 of the Limitation Act only when default on the part of the petitioners was not deliberate and the petitioners were not guilty of negligence and laches and the delay of each and every day has been sufficiently explained. In the instant case before me from the Supplementary-Affidavit and from the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act filed on behalf of the petitioners and also from submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners it is difficult to understand the exact number of days for which condonation of delay in filing revisional application was sought. In reply to a query raised by the Court, the learned Advocate for the petitioners failed to give any satisfactory or definite answer as to the number of days of delay occurred in filing the revisional application. In the circumstances, it appears that the petitioners are not sure as to the exact number of days of delay occurred in filing the revisional application for which they are seeking condonation of delay. It has been decided in a number of cases of this Court as well as the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that the delay of each and every day is to be explained satisfactorily before seeking relief under section 5 of the Limitation Act. In the instant case before me, the petitioners even do not know the exact number of days of delay in filing the revisional application. From the statement made in the application and the Supplementary-Affidavit it appears that the petitioners miserably failed to explain the delay of each and every day of 729 days. From a clear reading of the application for condonation of delay and the supplementary-affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioners one cannot get a clear idea as to the exact number of days of delay occurred in filing the revisional application for which the petitioners sought condonation of delay. However, in the instant case, the Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 to 7 to show cause as to why the delay of 729 days in filing the revisional application should not be condoned. This Court in disposing of this matter should confine itself within the terms of the rule issued wherein delay of 729 days has been mentioned. In that view of the matter, even if it is accepted that there was a delay of 729 days in filing the revisional application the defendants-petitioners are required to explain each and every day of delay. In the instant case, the petitioners failed to explain the delay of each and every day of 729 days. Mr ASM Wahidul Momin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that there is no statutory period for filing revisional application. In reply, Mr Nirmalendu Deb referred to the decision reported in 2 BLC (AD) 11 where the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court held that although the Limitation Act does not provide for any specific period of limitation for invoking revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure yet, for the long standing practice, one has to file it without causing inordinate delay, preferably within 90 days from the date of decree or order complained of. In appropriate case the High Court Division may suo motu exercise such jurisdiction.
